answer.rationale: The revision is cosmetic and responds only to peripheral reviewer comments (defining 5G, adding frequency bands, clarifying legal limits versus voluntary precaution, adding a Conclusion). The analyses, tables and interpretation are unchanged, so the central weaknesses remain. These are: the interpretation of effects that appeared only in the covariate-adjusted models; the conclusion that precaution does not harm trust, which rests on a non-significant result without equivalence testing; the validity of the novel practical-relevance measure and the relevance-before-treatment design; and the discrepancy between the abstract and the results (the abstract says only one RP measure rose, in Germany, while the results and Table 9 show the effects are mixed). The three reviewers raised no statistical concerns, and R1 explicitly disclaimed expertise on the methodology. The reviewer reports therefore did not test the central claims, and the unchanged manuscript still has the substantive problems below.

issues.issue: Treatment effects emerged only in the relevance-adjusted models (Germany affective RP, Greece trust at p=.047). They are interpreted as 'only visible' once relevance is controlled, and the finding is not integrated into the abstract or conclusion. The simple-slopes pattern (a text effect only at high relevance) is contrary to H3. Several tests are run with no multiplicity control, and the trust effect is borderline.
issues.response_claim: The amendments box says 'there are no major changes between the new version of the paper and the old one'. No analysis-related response was given.
issues.observed_change: The analyses are unchanged; Table 9 still carries footnote 2 on the affective RP and trust results.

evidence.exact_quote: the group differences regarding affective RP in Germany and regarding trust in Greece became only visible in our analysis when relevance was included
text condition (t = 2.0, p = .047) was a significant predictor, trust being higher in the precaution group

issues.issue: The Implications section claims precautionary information 'did not result in lower trust' and that this is 'good news'. This rests on non-significant results (Greece p=.06 in the H1/H2 model, in the opposite direction) with no equivalence test or confidence intervals. The self-efficacy mediation account is post hoc and untested, and the single-item exploratory measures are cross-sectional. The claim is stronger than the evidence allows.
issues.response_claim: A Conclusion subsection was added, and the response said 'The experimental design and methods are adequate'.
issues.observed_change: The added Conclusion restates results, but the 'good news' implication and the self-efficacy explanation are unchanged.

evidence.exact_quote: The finding that precautionary information did not result in lower trust compared to basic information may be good news for institutions

issues.issue: The practical-relevance measure (clicking on an article teaser) is novel and unvalidated, and it is correlated r≈.6 with the thematic measure. Relevance was measured before the treatment, so the question itself may prime the topic. The relevance quota in the sample may also distort the effects found. Panel quotas for age failed in Greece, and a fictional agency was used as the source, which limits external validity. None of this was addressed.
issues.response_claim: No response to this issue; R2's comments on exposure and awareness campaigns were answered by adding literature.
issues.observed_change: No change to the relevance measurement description or to its validity evidence.

evidence.exact_quote: It is too early to tell if our approach to use general interest in the topic as a proxy for personal relevance is helpful
it therefore needs to be considered that the older population is underrepresented

issues.issue: R1's objection was that precautionary advice amounts to the limits. The authors' clarification, that voluntary advice beyond legal limits is distinct, is reasonable and was visibly implemented in the introduction and discussion. R1 was a non-expert on the social-science side. R2's requests for frequencies and exposure were met with added text (FR1/FR2 bands, Greek exposure literature). The Greek exposure statement is only loosely related to the main inference.
issues.response_claim: 'we have revised the relevant passages to more clearly distinguish between legally enforced limits and voluntary precautionary behavior'; the 5G frequency bands were added.
issues.observed_change: The text now includes 'usually by legally enforcing limit values' and 'voluntary precautionary behavior that citizens can choose to take even when RF-EMF values are (far) below legal limits'. It also adds the FR1/FR2 bands and the Greek exposure citations.

evidence.exact_quote: voluntary precautionary behavior that citizens can choose to take even when RF-EMF values are (far) below legal limits
we have revised the relevant passages to more clearly distinguish between legally enforced limits and voluntary precautionary behavior

issues.issue: The abstract and conclusion state that precautionary information 'increased just one risk perception measure and only in Germany', which ignores the relevance-adjusted Germany affective RP effect, the Greece trust effect and the CR2 result. Numerical presentation is also inconsistent: Table 8 mixes standardized betas and unstandardized B, 'Multiple R' is labeled in the text and R² in the tables, and the Table 9 'CR2 precaution = CR2 precaution' row is mislabeled and hypothesis-decision labels are inconsistent. Gender coding with 'males=1' contradicts the 'females higher' sign descriptions. The 'six age ranges' are listed as five, and the Germany/Greece N values are swapped in Table 1 versus the text. The new Conclusion only restates the same headline.
issues.response_claim: The authors added a Conclusion section and said no major changes were made.
issues.observed_change: The Conclusion repeats the headline unchanged; the table and reporting inconsistencies were not corrected.

evidence.exact_quote: precautionary information increased only one measure of risk perception, and only in Germany

evidence.observation: Table 1 lists the final sample as 727 Germany / 721 Greece, but the sum rows show 735 and 727 left. Table 2 gives 727/721, matching the text only inconsistently.

evidence_limits: No raw data, the OSF materials, the full stimulus texts or the preregistration were available, so the analyses could not be rechecked and the exact stimuli could not be assessed.

The reviewer reports were thin: R1 disclaimed expertise on the methodology, and R2 and R3 gave short, positive, mostly peripheral comments. They therefore provide little independent checking of the statistics.
Judgement is limited to the supplied text, page images and responses; no external literature or later reports were consulted.
